analysis.one_liner: Halts new giant factory farms, forces meatpackers to buy more cattle on open markets, and restores origin labels.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote in either chamber and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have stopped new and expanding large factory farms (large CAFOs), phased out existing ones as of January 1, 2040, and paid farm owners to retire their debt and switch the land to other uses, funded at $10 billion a year. It would have made the big meat companies that contract with farmers legally responsible for the pollution and health harms those farms cause. It also would have rewritten the 1921 livestock competition law: packers would have to buy at least half their cattle and hogs through open, negotiated markets, limits would be placed on formula-priced contracts and on packers raising their own livestock, poultry companies could not use outside factors to rank farmers' pay, and beef, pork, and dairy would have to carry country-of-origin labels.
analysis.who_benefits: Family farmers and ranchers who sell on the open market, contract poultry and hog growers who face take-it-or-leave-it contracts, rural neighbors of factory farms dealing with manure and odors, and shoppers wanting to know where their meat comes from.

how_it_helps.text: Bars new large CAFOs from starting or expanding and requires existing large CAFOs to stop operating as large CAFOs after January 1, 2040, with civil penalties up to $10,000 per violation per day [S2][S3].

Creates a voluntary program paying farm owners to pay off debts on animal feeding operations and convert the property to pasture-based livestock, specialty crops, or organic production, funded by $10 billion per year transferred automatically from the Treasury [S2][S3].

Makes integrators — the corporations that supply chicks, feed, and instructions to contract growers — legally liable for dead animal and manure disposal, air and water pollution, harm to the contract grower, and damage to neighbors' health and property values, with attorney's fees for people who sue and win [S2][S3].

Requires covered meatpackers to buy at least 50% of the livestock they slaughter through open spot-market sales from independent producers, restricts forward and formula-priced contracts without firm base prices and open bidding, and bars most packers from owning or feeding livestock themselves [S2][S3].

Protects contract growers' legal rights, including the right to a jury trial, the right to see the data used to set their pay, and limits on the poultry 'tournament system' that ranks growers using factors the company controls [S3].

Restores mandatory country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork, extends it to dairy products, and reserves the 'Product of U.S.A.' label for meat from animals born, raised, and slaughtered in the United States [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large meatpacking companies, contract-farming integrators like Tyson and Purdue-style poultry operations, and operators of large factory farms, who face new liability, open-market purchase mandates, and the 2040 phase-out; taxpayers fund the $10 billion annual transition grants; some economists and industry groups warned the changes could raise meat prices and disrupt supply chains.

drawbacks.text: The transition program transfers $10 billion every year from the Treasury without a separate appropriation, a large ongoing taxpayer cost [S3].

Requiring half of slaughter volume to be bought through spot markets and restricting forward contracts would upend decades of contracted supply arrangements in cattle and hogs, which packers and some economists argued could raise consumer meat prices; a phase-out of large CAFOs by 2040 would reshape the meat supply system [S2][S3].
Joint permitting and broad integrator liability, including liability for neighbors' property-value and health claims, exposed agribusiness to potentially sweeping litigation risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles three things: real competition fixes for contract farmers (open-market purchase mandates, grower protections, origin labels), a pollution-and-liability crackdown on corporate-owned factory farms, and a very costly, disruptive managed phase-out of large CAFOs with a blank-check funding stream. The competition and liability provisions are the strongest case; the $10-billion-a-year transition fund and the 2040 mandate are the parts an honest supporter would have to defend against serious supply-chain and price questions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Agriculture Committee and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee on the day it was introduced, got sent to two subcommittees, and never received a markup, a vote, or a floor action before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna and 18 other Democrats introduced the Farm System Reform Act of 2023 on February 2, 2023 [S1][S3].
It was referred the same day to the House Agriculture Committee and the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee [S1][S5].
On February 3, 2023 it was sent to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee, and on March 6, 2023 to the Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; there was no committee markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote in the House or Senate before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1][S5].
The bill ended the Congress with 39 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large meatpacking companies, integrators, and large factory farm operators are better off, because the purchase mandates, liability rules, and phase-out were never debated or voted on. Status quo contracted supply chains remain intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large meatpackers and factory farm operators

for.name: Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on February 2, 2023 and recruited 18 original cosponsors and eventually 39 total.

for.name: 39 House cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, all Democrats including Pramila Jayapal, Jamie Raskin, and Jim McGovern
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; the bill never recorded any Republican cosponsors.

for.name: Senate companion sponsors and allied farmer, rural, and environmental groups
for.role: Outside supporters of the companion Farm System Reform Act
for.what_they_did: Publicly pushed the reform package, including country-of-origin labeling, that the House bill mirrored.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee (and its Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; never scheduled a markup or vote on it during the two-year Congress.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee; never acted on it.

against.name: Glenn Thompson
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee markup or vote during the 118th Congress.

against.name: Meatpacking, poultry, and large livestock industry groups
against.role: Meat processing and large-scale livestock industries
against.what_they_did: Opposed the CAFO moratorium, spot-market purchase mandates, packer ownership ban, and expanded country-of-origin labeling.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all 39 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors — and the Republican-chaired Agriculture Committee never gave the bill a vote [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Large meatpacking and poultry processing companies
industries.note: Would have had to buy at least half their livestock through open competitive bidding, face limits on formula-priced contracts and packer ownership of livestock, and lose the 'Product of U.S.A.' label on imported meat. Their interest in keeping the current closed contract system ran against independent producers' access to markets.

industries.industry: Integrators in contract livestock and poultry production
industries.note: Would have been made non-delegably liable for pollution, waste disposal, harm to growers, and damage to neighbors, and barred from pay-ranking growers using company-controlled factors. Their current structure shifts those costs onto growers and surrounding communities.

No new large factory farms could start or expand, and existing ones would have to cease operating as large CAFOs by January 1, 2040, with owners offered buyout and transition grants. Nearby rural residents bear the current odor, water, and health costs.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and hog producers
industries.note: Spot-market purchase requirements and the forward-contract rules would have restored open-market price discovery, which independent producers say gives them fairer prices; many ranch groups backed the labeling provisions.
Gained rights to compensation data, jury trial protections, attorney's fees, and protection from company-dominated pay tournaments, plus integrator liability for harms they currently absorb.

industries.industry: Meat importers and foreign-origin meat processors
industries.note: Lost the ability to label imported meat as 'Product of U.S.A.'; only animals born, raised, and slaughtered in the U.S. could carry it.
